name: Need 1000x More Qubits
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: From Hundreds to a Million: The Qubit Count Problem
lesson.summary: The largest quantum processors built so far have physical qubit counts in the hundreds to a bit over a thousand, while the earlier chapter on the million qubit requirement showed that a genuinely useful fault-tolerant algorithm is widely estimated to need somewhere in the rough ballpark of a million physical qubits, a gap of roughly a thousandfold.
lesson.body:
The earlier chapter on the million qubit requirement laid out why useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms need so many physical qubits, and it is worth reconnecting that target to where the actual hardware stands today, because the size of the gap is easy to underestimate. As of the most recent processors publicly reported by leading quantum computing companies, the largest devices have physical qubit counts on the order of hundreds up to a bit over a thousand. It is important to be precise about what that number means: these are raw, noisy physical qubits, the actual hardware components, not yet organized into the error-corrected logical qubits that a fault-tolerant algorithm actually runs on.

That distinction is exactly why the number needed is so much larger than the number available, and it connects directly back to the previous chapter on error rates. Because physical qubits are error-prone, a fault-tolerant computation cannot run directly on them, it has to run on logical qubits, each one built by combining many physical qubits together using a quantum error-correcting code so that the logical qubit's effective error rate is far lower than any individual physical qubit's error rate could achieve on its own. Depending on how far below the error threshold the physical qubits are operating, each logical qubit built this way might require anywhere from roughly a few hundred to well over a thousand physical qubits.

Then there is the separate question of how many logical qubits an actually useful algorithm needs. The commonly cited example in the research literature is using Shor's algorithm, the quantum algorithm for factoring large numbers, to break RSA-2048 encryption, a problem with genuine real-world stakes since RSA-2048 underlies a great deal of current cryptographic infrastructure. Published estimates for how many logical qubits this would take generally land in the range of a couple thousand to several thousand, plus a meaningful number of additional qubits for supporting operations.

Multiplying a needed logical qubit count in the thousands by a physical overhead per logical qubit in the hundreds to low thousands is where estimates for the total physical qubits required land, and here it is worth being direct about the range rather than pretending there is one settled number. Published estimates for factoring RSA-2048 specifically have varied, with some well-known analyses landing around twenty million physical qubits under their particular assumptions about error rates and the error-correcting code used, while other estimates, using different assumptions, land closer to the one million mark that gives this chapter its rough, order-of-magnitude figure. A commonly used round number in public discussion of the field is that a genuinely useful fault-tolerant quantum computer will need somewhere on the order of a million physical qubits, understood as a rough anchor point rather than a precise target, with real published estimates ranging from around that figure up into the tens of millions depending on how optimistic the assumptions about future error rates turn out to be. Compared against today's hardware, sitting in the hundreds to low thousands of physical qubits, that represents an increase of very roughly a thousandfold, which is the origin of the thousand times figure in this chapter's title.

It is worth stressing why qubit count alone is a seductive but incomplete headline metric, tying this directly back to the chapter on the required breakthroughs as a cluster. A processor with a thousand times more qubits than today, but without a matching improvement in error rates, would not actually be more useful, since it would simply have a thousand times more opportunities for uncorrected errors to accumulate. Progress on qubit count and progress on error rates have to happen together for either one to matter, which is exactly why the field treats them as separate, simultaneous required breakthroughs rather than treating a rising qubit count, on its own, as evidence that a useful machine is getting close.
